id: #104 from The Poems of Gaius Valerius Catullus

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

with Dana Ward with Dana Ward I have so little want of activity even writing with its pain more terrible than life I don’t want but do because I’m kind of stupid finally not in the way, you, Sarah know I am nor, you reader, who think of me fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait. Instruments for me are accessories, even the matchbook is only a tiara to my eyes, the fishing lure a long & white bracelet. Some of my so-called friends think of me as a derelict they always try to hold me to account. “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question” On the witness stand I am a kitten terribly cute but I can’t say a thing about stupid, or fish, or last night. I like to lay at the base of a hill asleep while the shepherds work bringing things to heel with tepid will where I source my contempt in the index of swill. The entries there make no mention of hell which was sifted through the vale of tears, & fell to make Earth, & the base of this hill where I sunbathe & murmur ‘jealous cellmate’ as my willful peers go by.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Dana, Ward, Sarah

outputs.L1:
**with Dana Ward**

with Dana Ward I have so little appetite for activity—even writing, with its pain more terrible than life, I do not desire, yet pursue nonetheless, because I am, in the end, rather foolish. Not foolish in the way you, Sarah, know me to be, nor as you, dear reader, imagine me, picturing me at my fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait. To me such instruments are mere accessories; even the matchbook is nothing but a tiara in my eyes, the fishing lure a long and white bracelet.

Some of my so-called friends regard me as a derelict, forever seeking to hold me to account. "Tell me what transpired on the drunken night in question." Upon the witness stand I am a kitten—terribly cute—yet I can utter nothing of foolishness, nor of fish, nor of last night.

I love to lie asleep at the foot of a hill while the shepherds labor, bringing things to heel with tepid will, and there I draw my contempt from the index of swill. Its entries make no mention of hell, which was sifted through the vale of tears, and fell to form the Earth—and the base of this very hill where I sunbathe and murmur "jealous cellmate" as my willful peers pass by.
outputs.L2:
alongside Dana Ward
alongside Dana Ward
I possess such minimal desire for motion
even the act of writing, whose pain
exceeds that of living itself
is something I resist yet perform anyway
because I'm foolish in a sense
not the sort of foolishness you recognize, Sarah
nor the kind you picture, reader
imagining me out there fishing.
The cord, the reel, the decoy, the bait.
To me these tools are mere ornaments,
even a book of matches becomes
nothing but a crown before my gaze,
the fishing decoy a slender pale bangle.
Certain people who claim to be my friends
regard me as a good-for-nothing
forever demanding explanations from me.
"Describe for us what occurred
on that intoxicated evening in question."
Seated in the witness box I'm a small cat,
dreadfully adorable, yet incapable
of uttering a word about foolishness,
about fish, or about the previous night.
I enjoy reclining at a hill's foot,
drifting to sleep while herders labor,
subduing creatures with their lukewarm resolve
there I draw my scorn
from the catalog of garbage.
Its listings say nothing of hell,
which was strained through the valley of weeping,
and dropped down to form the Earth,
and the foot of this same hill
where I bask in the sun and mutter
"envious prison-mate"
as my headstrong companions pass me by.
outputs.L3:
# On Idleness and Its Discontents

I confess to a profound aversion to activity of any kind—indeed, even the act of writing strikes me as more painful than living itself. And yet I persist, driven by nothing more noble than a stubborn sort of foolishness, continuing to set down words though every instinct rebels against the effort.

In my idleness, the ordinary objects of the world take on unexpected splendor. Common instruments and humble tools—the equipment of a fisherman, a simple book of matches—become in my imagination something far grander. I reimagine them as decorative finery: a tiara perched upon the brow, a bracelet clasped about the wrist. The mundane is transformed into the ornamental, as though the whole world were merely material for adornment.

My friends—if I may still call them such—regard me with less generosity. To them I am a derelict, a person fallen into ruin, and they take it upon themselves to hold me accountable, returning again and again to press me on the matter of my behavior. Their concern arrives dressed as interrogation.

When they question me thus, as though I stood in a witness box before some tribunal, I retreat into evasion. I become deliberately charming, coy, disarming—anything to deflect their scrutiny. I plead ignorance. I cannot explain myself, I tell them; I cannot account for my actions, nor give any honest reckoning of my drunken nights, which dissolve into a haze I claim no power to reconstruct.

For what I truly desire is only to rest, idle and undisturbed, at the base of some quiet hill. There I recline while my more industrious peers march past, busy with their purposeful lives. I feel, from some imagined "index of swill," the weight of contempt directed toward my indolence—a judgment I neither escape nor entirely resist, content to lie still beneath its scorn.
outputs.L4:
# On "with Dana Ward"

The poem "with Dana Ward" presents readers with a speaker who exists in deliberate tension with the act of creation itself. From its opening gestures, the poem establishes a persona who writes not out of inspiration or joy, but out of a reluctant compulsion—one that causes genuine discomfort. This paradox, of a writer who finds writing painful yet continues nonetheless, forms the emotional core around which the poem's other concerns orbit. The speaker does not romanticize the creative struggle; rather, they expose it as a wearying obligation, one they undertake with visible ambivalence.

Central to the poem's imaginative texture is the speaker's peculiar habit of transforming ordinary, utilitarian objects into things of decorative or aesthetic significance. Fishing lures, matchbooks, and similar mundane artifacts are lifted from their practical contexts and reimagined as ornaments or accessories. This act of recontextualization does more than demonstrate the speaker's idiosyncratic vision; it signals a fundamental resistance to using things—and by extension, oneself—for their intended, productive purposes. The lure that no longer lures, the matchbook that no longer lights, become emblems of a broader refusal to participate in systems of function and utility.

Formally, the poem enacts its themes through fragmentation. Rather than proceeding through orderly argument or narrative, the verse moves in disconnected images, resisting the coherence that a reader might expect or demand. This structural quality mirrors the speaker's own resistance to accountability. Just as the poem declines to resolve into tidy meaning, the speaker declines to justify themselves, to explain their choices, or to submit to any standard of legibility. The persona is, in this sense, unreliable—not because they deceive, but because they refuse the very premise that they owe anyone a clear or consistent account of their inner life.

What emerges from this constellation of gestures is a defiant philosophy of idleness. The speaker's apathy is not passive or accidental; it is cultivated and deliberate, positioned pointedly against the expectations of "willful peers"—those who embody ambition, discipline, and conventional productivity. Against their industry, the speaker sets contempt and indolence, embracing these ordinarily disparaged states as forms of quiet rebellion. To do nothing, to want nothing, to refuse the machinery of achievement, becomes in this poem a kind of stance, even a kind of integrity.

Ultimately, "with Dana Ward" articulates alienation not as suffering to be pitied but as a chosen orientation toward the world. The speaker's estrangement from mainstream values, from productivity, and even from the pleasures of their own writing, is reframed as a subtle act of defiance. In elevating idleness and contempt to the level of principle, the poem challenges the reader to reconsider what social judgment demands of us, and whether the refusal to comply might itself constitute a meaningful, if uncomfortable, form of freedom.

**An Unexpected Reunion**

Dana hurried down the hospital corridor, searching for the right room number. Her sister had called earlier that morning with the news—their childhood friend had been admitted overnight.

When she finally reached Ward 7, Dana paused at the entrance, taking a deep breath before stepping inside. The room was quiet except for the soft beeping of monitors.

"Dana? Is that really you?" came a weak voice from the bed.

"Sarah!" Dana rushed forward, tears welling up in her eyes. "I came as soon as I heard. How are you feeling?"

Sarah managed a smile despite her obvious exhaustion. "Better now that you're here. It's been what, ten years?"

"Too long," Dana replied, pulling a chair close to the bedside. "I should have reached out sooner. Life just got so busy after college."

They spent the next few hours catching up, sharing memories of their teenage adventures and filling in the gaps of the past decade. Sarah spoke about her career as a teacher, while Dana described her travels abroad.

As afternoon light streamed through the window of Ward 7, both women realized that some friendships, no matter how much time passes, can pick up right where they left off.

"Promise me we won't wait another ten years," Sarah said, squeezing Dana's hand.

"I promise," Dana whispered.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness poem in the voice of a lazy, self-deprecating narrator who addresses both a friend named Sarah and the reader, using fishing imagery and themes of contempt, idleness, and being held to account.
counterfactuals.output:
**Slack Line**

Sarah, I meant to cast the line at dawn—
you know I did, or you don't, why would you,
I'm the kind of man who lets the reel go soft,
lets the whole tangled morning drift downstream
while I sit here explaining myself to you,
reader, whoever you are, hunched over this
like it's a catch worth keeping.

Look at me. Don't. There's nothing in the bucket
but the smell of what I might have done.
Sarah, you always baited your own hooks,
you always came home slick with silver,
and I'd be on the dock still testing the wind
with a wet finger, contemptuous
of the fish, the rod, the whole wet business,
mostly of the arm that won't lift it.

You ask what I did today. That's the worst part—
that anyone asks, that the ledger opens,
that somewhere a hand keeps score
of the worms I did not thread, the lakes
I stood beside and slandered.
I called the water lazy. Rich, I know.
I, who am the still spot where nothing bites.

And you, reader, you're worse than Sarah,
you're patient, you wait to see if I'll
haul something up, some meaning, some fish
with a coin in its mouth, and I won't,
I'll just keep feeding you the line, the slack,
the almost, the tomorrow-for-sure.

Sarah, hold me to account if you want.
Stand on the bank with your arms crossed.
I'll watch my own float bob and do nothing,
loving nothing, least of all the man
who could have, at any moment, simply
pulled.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem titled "with Dana Ward" that mimics the associative, conversational style of contemporary poets like Dana Ward—rambling, intimate, philosophical, with sudden shifts between mundane objects and cosmic imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
with Dana Ward

We were talking about the color of gas station light,
how it makes everyone look recently arrived
from a great distance, and Dana said the word "provisional"
the way you'd hold a moth by the wings, carefully,
so as not to smudge whatever makes it fly, and I thought
about my mother folding towels, the specific competence
of her hands, how she died before I could tell her
the towels were beautiful, that ordinary care
is the only religion I've managed to keep,
and somewhere a satellite is falling back to earth
in pieces smaller than a thought, and we're standing
in the parking lot of the everything, holding coffees
that have gone the temperature of the air,
which is to say the temperature of forgetting,
and Dana laughs at something I don't remember saying,
and this is the whole of it, isn't it, the friendship
that survives its own conversation, the way light
keeps arriving from stars that quit millennia ago,
so that when I look up I'm reading a letter
from the dead, addressed to no one, saying only
here, here, here, the same word the heart makes
when it's just being a heart, when it forgets
its terrible job and simply keeps time
the way a kid keeps a secret, badly, joyfully,
telling everyone. The cars go by. A dog
somewhere has opinions. And I want to say to you,
whoever finds this, that we were here,
that we stood in the failing light and talked
about nothing, which is the largest of the subjects,
that Dana bought me a candy bar from the machine
and it was the tenderness of empires, the whole
economy of touch reduced to sixty cents
and the small gift of it, unwrapped and shared
under a sky that couldn't care less and cares
in the way that mattering doesn't require a witness—
and then we drove home separately,
into our separate weathers, each of us
a small lit window someone might be passing,
thinking, someone lives there, someone
is awake in there, being alive, doing the dishes,
missing the dead, forgiving the light for leaving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental free-verse poem where the speaker resists activity and writing, imagines themselves as a cute kitten on a witness stand, lounges at the base of a hill, and reflects on hell, the vale of tears, and jealousy.
counterfactuals.output:
**Deposition at the Foot of the Hill**

I would rather not.

That's the poem. That's the testimony.
I am refusing the verb, I am declining
the gerund, I am a kitten sworn in
on a witness stand, one paw raised,

*do you swear* — mew —
*the whole truth* — I lick between my toes,
I have never been so cute,
I have never known less.

Objection. Sustained. I nap.

*

The hill is behind me and I will not climb it.
Somewhere up there is the activity,
the doing, the being-seen-to-do,
and here at the base I am lounging
like punctuation the sentence forgot,

a comma in the grass,
a soft withholding.

*

They told me the world is a vale of tears
and I believe them, I do,
but the vale is also where you lie down,
belly to the cool of it,
and the tears water something
that has no name and does not ask.

Hell, I think, is a hill you are told to climb
forever, and forever being told,
and forever the small voice that says
*someone else is already at the top,*

and that voice is jealousy,
green as a kitten's eye,
green as the hill I refuse,
green as the thing I will not become.

*

Reconvene the court.
The witness has curled into a circle.
The witness will not testify.
The witness is the whole truth:

I would rather not,
and rather-not is the softest hell,
the one with sun in it,
the one where the tears
have finally, finally
stopped being asked to mean.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a modern poem in the New York School tradition that blends drunken confession, self-mockery, fishing metaphors, and mythological cosmology, addressed to a specific named person.
counterfactuals.output:
# Letter to Frank at the End of a Bad Cast

Frank, I'm drunk again and thinking
of how Poseidon must have felt
that first time he threw his net
and pulled up nothing but the moon's
reflection, wet and useless as my ambitions.

You'd laugh at me here, elbow-deep
in cheap Chablis and cheaper metaphors,
casting lines into the kitchen sink
where no fish live, where nothing lives
except the dishes I've abandoned
like a fleet of lesser Argos.

Remember when I said I'd be somebody?
The gods are laughing, Frank.
Zeus with his big dumb thunderbolt
couldn't hit the ocean if he tried,
and neither can I hit the note
I keep reaching for in this poem,
this glass, this life that hooks me
by the lip and reels me in.

I am the worst fisherman in Manhattan.
I've caught three colds and one bad marriage
and a sadness shaped exactly like Ohio.
You always knew which flies to tie,
which lies to tell the trout,
while I stood dumb as Prometheus
waiting for the eagle of my own bad choices
to arrive on schedule, punctual as rent.

The thing about mythology, Frank,
is that everyone's already dead
and still they won't stop drowning.
Narcissus in his pond. Me in mine.
The bourbon says I love you
in a way I never could sober,
which is to say completely,
which is to say like a hook
loves the soft interior of the mouth.

It's 3 AM and Neptune's chariot
is just the garbage truck again,
grinding up the avenue,
collecting all the small gods
we threw away this week.
I'll be one of them soon enough—
tossed back, too small to keep,
swimming off into whatever dark
water holds the likes of us,

the ones who cast and cast
and only catch the reflection
of the thing we wanted,
you, old friend, already
on the other shore,
waving, or maybe drowning,
it's too far now to tell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that begins by repeating a name, uses run-on syntax, treats everyday items like matchbooks and fishing lures as jewelry, and ends with an image of a speaker sunbathing while murmuring about a "jealous cellmate."
counterfactuals.output:
**Ledger, Ledger**

Ledger, Ledger, you keep coming back to me
the way a smell does, uninvited, wearing yesterday around your neck like it were something
precious, and I have been collecting too, look,
these matchbooks pinned along my collarbone, each one struck
and re-struck, sulfur pearls, a rosary of little fires
I never lit for God, and the fishing lures, oh
the fishing lures, barbed and feathered, dangling from my ears
like the earrings of a woman who has drowned three husbands and buried
none of them, only wore them, only glittered
harder in the wet, and I keep talking, I know, I keep
running the sentence past the exit, past the shoulder, past the last
gas station of good sense because to stop
is to admit the sun is going, and it isn't, it isn't,
it's noon forever on this concrete slab of a life
where I lie back, oiled and shining, my jewelry
of hooks and spent matches catching light,
and murmur to the fence, to the wire, to no one,
about my jealous cellmate, how she covets
my ridiculous treasure, how she'd trade her name for mine,
how even here, even now, someone still wants
to be me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
